claim: Buerger and Hogan propose a computational loop-shaping procedure for interaction controllers that separates robot-port performance from coupled stability, searches controller pole/zero/gain space, and constrains the search either by passivity or by a less conservative complementary-stability condition. Complementary stability models the expected human-arm environment as a bounded set and converts stable coupling with every member of that set into a robust-stability test using the small-gain theorem and structured singular value. On one screw-driven single-DOF rehabilitation-robot module, the selected low-frequency lag force-feedback controller reduced Coulomb friction from 10-20 N to below 0.5 N and apparent inertia from 6 kg to 1.2 kg while passing the reported spring, hard-block, and human-arm tests more robustly than tested natural-admittance alternatives. The evidence supports the design idea and this actuator case, but not general multi-DOF human-robot safety: the environment set, linear robot model, controller family, single module, bandwidth limits, and non-statistical human testing sharply bound the conclusion.
claim_locator: Section V, Figures 14-15 and Tables I-II
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical and robot-hardware evidence: the port-model design logic and bounded-environment robust-stability formulation are directly documented, and large impedance reductions are measured on one single-DOF module; no statistical human study, clinical outcome, multi-DOF validation, or universal interaction-safety certificate is provided
problem_and_setting: High-force human-interactive robots require low and tunable endpoint impedance together with high force capacity. Force feedback can suppress friction and inertia but threatens coupled stability. Classical servo loop-shaping tools do not transfer directly because robot-port performance depends on robot impedance alone, whereas stability depends on the robot-environment port-function product, and controller dynamics are embedded nonlinearly in robot impedance. The concrete platform is one screw-driven linear module intended for rehabilitation robotics.
method_or_mechanism: The method defines a frequency-domain cost from deviation between actual and target robot-port impedance and separately imposes a coupled-stability constraint. For a chosen controller structure, a computational grid searches pole, zero, and gain; at each pole-zero combination it finds the largest admissible gain and displays a design surface. First, positive-real port impedance enforces passivity. Then complementary stability replaces the all-passive-environments requirement with a set of expected environments represented by a nominal port function plus bounded uncertainty. For human arms, a second-order mass-spring-damper model with bounded real parameter deviations is used. The robot is inverted to admittance form and structured singular value/small-gain analysis tests robust stability across that environment set. This permits selected nonpassive controllers when their destabilizing environments lie outside the modeled set.
content_summary: The paper first explains why interaction design differs structurally from ordinary servo design. It then applies computational loop shaping to a linear single-resonance model of a screw-driven robot with handle force-sensor dynamics. Under passivity, the search finds low-frequency lag/PI force compensation superior to proportional control for friction rejection. Complementary stability uses bounded human-arm inertia, damping, and stiffness from prior literature and identifies both lag and high-frequency lead regions with lower impedance cost than the passive design; the implemented high-frequency lead design was precluded by force-measurement bandwidth. A 1 kHz lag controller was tested against springs, a hard block, and vigorous human-arm grasp. Model predictions were conservative, possibly because unmodeled Coulomb friction dissipated energy. The controller was compared with natural admittance control and gave the better reported stability-performance combination on this platform. The conclusion identifies extension to multi-DOF/configuration-dependent systems as unresolved.
synthesis_role: Represents an early explicit relaxation of universal passivity: controller design uses a bounded task/environment class to gain performance while retaining robust coupled stability for that class. It is a conceptual predecessor to environment-aware robust interaction design and constrained optimization of impedance policies.
development_link: Compared with proportional force feedback and passive natural admittance, the method shapes feedback frequency response and searches the stability-performance surface. Compared with passivity, complementary stability is less conservative but only as trustworthy as the bounded environment model. Compared with later energy-tank or certificate-constrained variable impedance, it is an offline linear frequency-domain design for a fixed controller on a single-DOF actuator.

evidence.finding: Robot-port behavior determines interaction performance, while the robot-environment port-function product determines coupled stability; controller transfer functions do not enter these quantities as simple multiplicative loop-shaping factors.

A frequency-weighted impedance-error cost and passivity constraint are evaluated over pole-zero-gain grids; for the modeled module, low-frequency lag/PI compensation reduces impedance more effectively than proportional feedback while remaining passive.

Complementary stability requires robust stability for all environments in a bounded set; a second-order human-arm model with bounded mass, damping, and stiffness is tested using small-gain/structured-singular-value analysis.

Relaxing passivity to the bounded human-environment set lowers the best plotted normalized impedance cost from 0.72 to 0.50 and identifies nonpassive lag and lead controller regions predicted stable for the modeled set.

The selected lag controller ran at 1 kHz on one screw-driven single-DOF robot module; contact and impact tests used six springs, a hard plastic block, and vigorous human-arm grasp, while high-frequency lead compensation could not be implemented because of force-measurement bandwidth.
The implemented lag compensator reduced measured Coulomb friction from 10-20 N to below 0.5 N and apparent inertia from 6 kg to 1.2 kg, below the 3 kg passive limit stated for the model.

Within the tested spring, block, and arm conditions, the lag controller was more robust than the tested natural-admittance alternatives at comparable low-impedance performance; complete numeric table cells are poorly recovered from the supplied PDF text layer, so only the paper's stated comparison is retained.

The authors report a primitive optimization search and single-DOF application; extending the method to multi-DOF, configuration-dependent actuator or endpoint dynamics is nontrivial and left for further work.

boundary_conditions: The analytical and experimental system is linearized and single-DOF with one dominant structural resonance and handle force-transducer dynamics.

Complementary stability guarantees coupling only with the explicitly modeled bounded environment set; an environment outside its mass, damping, stiffness, or structural assumptions may destabilize the nonpassive controller.

The human arm is represented as a second-order passive-like mechanical environment from prior literature; voluntary activation, reflex delay, multi-joint configuration changes, nonlinearity, and active devices are not comprehensively modeled.
The reported human-arm test is a vigorous grasp test without a stated cohort, protocol statistics, or adverse-event analysis; it is not clinical or population-level evidence.
The high-frequency lead controller identified in analysis was not implemented because force-sensor bandwidth was inadequate.
The robot model omits substantial Coulomb friction; the authors infer this may explain conservative stability predictions, but unmodeled dissipation cannot be assumed under all operating conditions.
Controller search is restricted to a chosen low-order pole-zero-gain family and frequency-domain cost; global optimality over controller structures is not established.
The natural-admittance comparison uses one platform and tested parameter sets rather than a general controlled benchmark.
No collision-force, tissue-load, fault, actuator-saturation, or multi-contact safety constraint is certified.
assumptions: The linear robot/force-sensor model contains the dominant instability-producing dynamics over the design band.
The impedance-magnitude cost over the selected log-spaced frequencies is a meaningful proxy for perceived or task-relevant low-impedance performance.
The bounded second-order environment set contains every human arm/environment the controller will encounter in its intended use.
Structured-singular-value calculations and the sampled frequency grid detect the relevant robust-stability boundary.
The implemented 1 kHz controller, sensing, and actuator reproduce the model closely enough that offline stability predictions remain informative.
The spring, block, and grasp tests are sufficiently exciting to expose unstable interaction for the tested conditions.
Measured friction and apparent inertia from slow force-position and initial-condition tests generalize to the relevant task amplitudes and velocities.

reported: Proportional endpoint force feedback that reduces apparent inertia too aggressively becomes nonpassive and vulnerable to contact instability.
Classical servo loop-shaping does not map transparently to interaction control because stability and performance depend on different port-function quantities.
The high-frequency lead controller could not be implemented on the hardware because of force-measurement bandwidth.
Natural admittance can drift in stiffness rendering because it feeds back velocity rather than position.
Nonpassive natural-admittance settings were less robust in the reported tests; settings matching lag-controller stability retained high inertia/damping and poorer performance.
The method had only been applied to single-DOF systems, and multi-DOF/configuration-dependent extension was unresolved.
inferred: If the environment uncertainty set is misspecified, complementary stability can authorize a nonpassive controller that is unstable with a plausible unmodeled person, tool, fixture, or contact geometry.
Coarse parameter/frequency grids can miss narrow instability regions or better controller structures.
Unmodeled Coulomb friction can mask instability during testing and may change with temperature, wear, lubrication, velocity, or load.
A pass/fail grasp test with an unspecified human sample cannot establish robustness across anthropometry, pathology, activation, or involuntary reflexes.
The large impedance reductions on one actuator do not directly imply safe or transparent behavior after integration into a multi-axis robot.
Robust coupled stability is not equivalent to task safety, comfort, clinical benefit, collision safety, or fault tolerance.
